tour.title: Markets, Food & Neon
tour.summary: A market street, an electric town and a canal of signs — two and a half kilometres across the merchant city that fed Japan, ending at a moss-covered statue in a surviving prewar lane.
tour.overviewText:
Osaka's oldest joke about itself is that you should eat until you go bankrupt. The word is kuidōraku — kui, to eat, dō, to ruin — and the full proverb runs: ruin yourself on clothes in Kyoto, ruin yourself on food in Osaka. It is a merchant city's boast, and everything on this walk was built by the trade that made the boast true.

Here is the machinery. For two and a half centuries Japan was ruled from Edo — today's Tokyo — by the Tokugawa shoguns, and Osaka, a port at the mouth of the Yodo river system, was where the country's wealth actually moved. Rice was money: samurai were paid in it, rents were collected in it, taxes were assessed in it. Feudal lords shipped their harvests here to sell and stored them in warehouses along the canals, and in 1697 the brokers of the Dōjima district formalised a market in rice that had not yet been delivered — trading paper contracts on future harvests, which is why the Dōjima Rice Exchange is treated as a forerunner of the modern futures market. Osaka became tenka no daidokoro, the nation's kitchen: the place that priced, stored and shipped what everyone ate. The nickname is not a foodie compliment. It is an economic fact with a chef's accent.

What that produced is a city with an unusual social contract. Osaka had no imperial court and no shogun in residence, so status came from the deal rather than the title, and the cooking grew cheap, fast, and performed in front of you on a hot iron plate. Locals will tell you Tokyo is stiff and Kyoto is precious; Osaka is the one that talks to strangers. In February that means crab, in from the northern Sea of Japan and the San'in coast, and oysters at their winter best — and it means the neon along the canal is at its most useful, because darkness is when Dōtonbori makes sense.

This walk is about two and a half kilometres in total — short hops between the stops, apart from one long unguided stretch of some 1.5 kilometres through the Namba grid, for which there is a metro shortcut if you want it. You start by eating your way down a covered market street, cut through Osaka's electric town, walk a roofed shopping arcade down to the canal, and finish in a lane of lanterns and one improbable statue. With the eating, budget most of a day; every stop is also a meal.

Useful before you start: the currency is the yen, written ¥, and small stalls still prefer cash. Hours and prices at markets move constantly — treat every number here as a rough guide and check at the stall. Come on a weekday if you can; the market is a workplace first, and it opens early and shuts early.

Come hungry. That is the whole point.
tour.difficulty: Easy: flat, paved and step-free the whole way, with one long unguided stretch of about 1.5 km through ordinary city streets between the electric town and the shopping arcade. The real difficulty is crowds — the arcade and the canal are shoulder-to-shoulder after dark and on weekends, and a covered market street is narrow. Everything is on tarmac or flagstone; no stairs are required at any stop.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at the market around 9 to 10am, when the fish counters are still stocked and the aisles are navigable, and work south through Den Den Town in the early afternoon. Reach Shinsaibashi-suji by mid-afternoon, the canal by dusk, and the Glico sign and Hozenji Yokocho after dark — that is when Dōtonbori earns its reputation. Avoid Sunday at the market, when a number of stalls shut, and expect the market to be largely closed by early evening.

stops.name: Kuromon Ichiba Market
stops.narration:
You are standing in a Japanese covered market, which is not a building full of stalls but a street with, for most of its length, a roof laid over it — here about 580 metres of it running north to south, lined with roughly 150 shops. The name is the history: kuromon means black gate, and this market began around 1822 beside the black gate of Enmyōji temple, where merchants sold fish brought up from Sakai and the Kishu coast. The temple burned down in the Great Namba fire of 1912 and the market burned again in the air raids of 1945; both times it was rebuilt on the same street. Until the temple went, this was the Enmyōji market.

What makes Kuromon different from a food hall is who else shops here. Osaka's professional chefs — itamae, the trained cooks of sushi counters and of kaiseki, the formal multi-course Japanese dinner — still come for the morning fish, and a market that must satisfy them cannot survive on tourists alone. About 18,000 people pass through on a weekday; at the end of December, when Japan buys its festive food, that figure reaches into the hundreds of thousands.

Eat while you are here, and eat standing at the stall. The small pan-fried rolled omelette called tamagoyaki is the traditional starter, sweet and faintly dashi-flavoured — dashi being the stock of dried kelp and bonito flakes that underlies nearly all Japanese savoury cooking. Then oysters in winter, grilled scallops, skewers of wagyū beef, sea urchin and salmon roe over rice, and whatever the cold case is pushing. Look for fugu, the pufferfish, which is lethally toxic in the wrong hands and therefore must by law be butchered by a licensed chef — an expensive ritual elsewhere in Japan, sold here by the piece. February is exactly the season for it.

Now the honest part. Nobody is obliged to give you local prices, and several stalls have quietly become tourist counters: you will find a small, chewy beef skewer for ¥2,000 and a slice of melon for ¥1,000 and more. The stalls with a queue of office workers are usually the fair ones. As a rule, do not eat while walking down the middle of the arcade — buy, step to the side or into the stall's own standing counter, eat there, and keep the lane clear. A wholesale street is somebody's workplace and the fish crates do not wait for photographers. Most stalls open around 8 or 9am, many shut between 4:30 and 6pm, a few restaurants run later, many shops close on Sundays and holidays, and cutting boards come down early on Wednesdays in some places — verify at the stall. Bring cash; a growing number of shops take cards and transport IC cards, but not all do.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the market. Food is priced per stall — reckon on ¥2,000 to ¥4,000 a head for a real graze, more if you chase wagyū or sea urchin. Tourist-facing stalls charge tourist prices; verify at the counter before you commit.
stops.openingHours: The street itself is public at all hours. Most stalls run roughly 8:00 to 17:00 or 18:00, a few fish dealers open before dawn, some restaurants later. Many shops close Sundays and holidays. Hours move — confirm at the stall.
stops.accessibility: Level and paved throughout, and much of the long street sits under an arcade roof, though not all of it. It is narrow and busy: crowds make wheelchairs and strollers slow going around 11:00 to 14:00. No public seating; eating is standing at counters.
stops.insiderTip: Judge a stall by who is queuing. If the line is chefs and local shoppers, the price is honest; if it is all suitcases and selfie sticks, you are paying a premium for the photograph. Buy it, step out of the walking lane, and eat it at the counter before you move on.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the market at its south end and turn right onto Sakaisuji, the broad avenue with the elevated road overhead — that is the spine of Den Den Town, and the electric town begins almost immediately. Walk south for about 400 metres, past the second-hand tool shops and the electronics windows, until the signs are thick and stacked three deep. That corner is your next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: ERIC SALARD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Nipponbashi Den Den Town
stops.narration:
Welcome to Electric Town. The locals call it Den Den Town, short for denki no machi — electric town — and it is Osaka's answer to Tokyo's Akihabara. It has the same origin story as almost every such district in Japan: after the war, when new consumer goods were scarce, small shops began selling radio valves and spare parts to people repairing sets by hand. In Osaka that trade settled on this stretch of Sakaisuji avenue from the late 1940s, and it never left. Today it sells computers, cameras, audio gear, electronic components, machine tools — and, on the upper floors, the anime, manga, games, model kits and character goods that make it the otaku district of western Japan.

Otaku is a Japanese word for someone whose enthusiasm for one subject — usually anime, games or idols — runs far past a hobby. It is not a polite word everywhere, but in Osaka it is a business model, and this street is its marketplace.

Two things distinguish Den Den Town from Akihabara. First, the geography: Akihabara is tall and stacked, a warren of multi-floor buildings; Den Den Town is long and shallow, two parallel shopping streets — the covered Nipponbashi-suji arcade along Sakaisuji and the narrower Ota-dōri one block east — which makes it far easier to walk and far less frantic. Second, the haggling. Negotiable prices are a Kansai habit that Tokyo largely lost; ask politely and you may be surprised. Some shops are tax-free for foreign visitors, which means you show your passport and skip the 10 per cent consumption tax, though this is the shop's concession rather than a right, so check the sign.

Look at the ground under your feet while you are here: this was an Edo-period staging post called Nagamachi, on the road heading south out of the city, and it was renamed Nipponbashi in 1872 — sharing its name with Tokyo's Nipponbashi bridge district, which is why the two are usually kept apart in conversation as Osaka-Nipponbashi and Tokyo-Nipponbashi. In the Meiji and Taishō eras the street was known for second-hand bookshops; a few still survive in the back lanes between the two avenues, alongside decades-old cafés and hardware shops that never got round to modernising.

A practical note for the rest of your day: the trade here has partly moved on. The big electronics chains opened huge branches in Umeda and Sennichimae, and browsing moved online, so some of what you see is a district performing its own history. What has grown back in its place is the pop culture — maid cafés where staff dress as anime characters and serve tea, card shops, retro game stores.

Shop hours are typically around 10:00 or 11:00 until 19:00 or 20:00, with several shops closed on irregular weekdays, so a morning visit may find shutters down; verify as you go. Nothing here is a ticketed sight — it is a shopping street, free to walk, and the only cost is whatever you carry home.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the district; it is a shopping street. Anything you buy is at shop prices, and some shops offer tax-free purchase to foreign visitors on presentation of a passport — ask at the counter.
stops.openingHours: Individual shops, not the district. Most run roughly 11:00 to 20:00, with some opening at 10:00 and a number closed on irregular weekdays. The street is public at all hours. Check each shopfront.
stops.accessibility: Level, step-free along both Sakaisuji and Ota-dōri, with a covered arcade along Sakaisuji. Streets are wide enough for wheelchairs; shop interiors vary and many small shops are cramped or have a step at the door.
stops.insiderTip: Walk Ota-dōri, the narrower parallel street one block east, for the odd corners: tiny Shōwa-era cafés, pawn and recycle shops, old hardware stores. Then look for the few surviving second-hand bookshops in the lanes between the two avenues, the district's original trade.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the middle of Den Den Town, head west along Sennichimae-dōri past the Namba station complex, then turn north and keep going until you meet the roof laid over the street — about 1.5 km in all, roughly twenty minutes at a stroll, and it is the one unguided stretch of this walk. If you would rather ride it, take the Osaka Metro Sennichimae Line one stop from Nippombashi to Namba and change to the Midosuji Line one stop to Shinsaibashi, about ¥190 a ride, then follow the signs up into the arcade. Either way you arrive under the glass roof of Shinsaibashi-suji.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Fabio Achilli from Milano, Italy, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Shinsaibashi-suji Arcade
stops.narration:
Look up. That glass barrel roof is the whole idea. Shinsaibashi-suji is a shōtengai — a Japanese commercial street, closed to cars and, here, roofed for its entire length — and it runs roughly 600 metres dead straight, from the Shinsaibashi station end about two hundred metres behind you down to the canal, with about 180 shops under the arch. The roof is not decoration. Osaka's summers are brutally humid and its typhoon-season rain is heavy, and a covered street keeps shoppers shopping in both.

The name is older than the shopping. It belongs to a merchant: Okada Shinsai, who helped dig the Nagahori canal here in 1622 and built the bridge that took his name. Merchants have traded on this line ever since; the arcade you are standing in is the latest roof over a very old counter.

Understand what a shōtengai is and you understand a great deal of ordinary Japan. After the war these streets were the commercial spine of every neighbourhood, run by shopkeeper associations that paid for the roof, the lights and the festivals, and they served people who lived within walking distance: the fishmonger, the rice dealer, the barber, the knife sharpener. Most of those neighbourhood associations have shrunk as supermarkets and then the internet took their trade, and Japan now has thousands of half-empty shōtengai. Shinsaibashi-suji survived by being too central to fail — but look at what filled the shopfronts. The knife shop and the rice dealer are gone; in their place are global fashion chains, drugstores, cosmetics shops and the sort of dessert counter that exists mainly to be photographed. That is not decay, exactly, but it is a swap, and it tells you which way the money flows.

Two details worth noticing. First, the crowd runs in one direction in the morning and the other in the evening, because the arcade is really a pedestrian route connecting the Shinsaibashi shopping district to Namba. Second, eating while walking is frowned on here — not rudely enforced, but the polite habit is to buy and stand, or sit, before you move on, and the same goes for the market you have just left. Small civilities are how a street this crowded stays workable.

Shops generally open around 10:00 or 11:00 and close around 20:00 or 21:00, with restaurants running later; individual shops set their own hours and some close on a fixed weekday. Walking the arcade costs nothing, and there is no ticket and no gate. Everything depends on what you decide to buy — verify prices as you go, and carry your passport if you intend to shop, since tax-free counters need it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk — it is a shopping street, not a sight. Shops set their own prices; tax-free purchase for visitors requires your passport and is at each shop's discretion.
stops.openingHours: Public at all hours. Most shops open around 10:00 to 11:00 and close around 20:00 to 21:00; restaurants later. Some shops close one weekday. Busiest from late afternoon into the evening.
stops.accessibility: Excellent for access: level, paved, fully covered, step-free for the whole length, with lifts and escalators from the subway concourse below. Very crowded in the afternoons and at weekends, which is the only real obstacle.
stops.insiderTip: One block west is Midosuji, the wide boulevard with the luxury flagships and a fraction of the crowd. Walk down the arcade for the density and the ordinary Japanese shops, then come back north on Midosuji for the space — you see both Osakas in twenty minutes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Keep walking south down the arcade and do not turn off; about 400 metres ahead the roof ends and the street spills onto Ebisubashi bridge over the Dōtonbori canal. Stop in the middle of the bridge and turn to face the water. That is your next stop, and it is the view everyone came for.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: そらみみ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Dōtonbori Canal & Ebisubashi Bridge
stops.narration:
You are standing on a bridge built for a shrine, standing over a canal dug by a man who died in a war and never saw it finished. Take them in order.

The canal is the older thing. In 1612 a local administrator named Nariyasu Dōton began cutting it along the southern edge of the city, and he died in the summer of 1615 during the Siege of Osaka — the campaign in which the Tokugawa shoguns finally destroyed the Toyotomi family and took uncontested control of Japan. His partners finished the canal that September. The new lord of Osaka Castle, Matsudaira Tadaaki, named it after him anyway, Dōtonbori, with bori from hori, a canal. So the most famous name in Osaka belongs to a man on the losing side, remembered by the winner — which, in a merchant city, tells you something about how useful a good name is.

The name on the bridge is different. Ebisubashi is the bridge of Ebisu, one of the seven lucky gods of Japanese folk belief and the patron of fishermen and of business generally, whose shrine at Imamiya lies off to the south-west; this was the road to it. The first bridge went up in 1615 with the canal. What you are crossing is the 2007 rebuild, the latest in a line that includes a steel version from 1878 and a concrete arch from 1925, and it is only about 26 metres long — you can walk it in ten steps and spend an hour on it.

Now look around, because everything visible here is a decision made about what Osaka is. In 1621 the shogunate formally designated this district as the city's entertainment quarter, and by 1662 it held six kabuki theatres and five bunraku theatres — kabuki being the spectacular song-and-dance drama of the stage, bunraku the half-life-size puppet theatre that Japan perfected, with three operators visibly working one puppet. The playhouses are gone; almost all were destroyed in the 1945 bombings. What replaced them in the twentieth century was advertising, and Osaka turned out to be exceptionally good at it.

The canal itself had a long, unglamorous working life carrying cargo, and by the 1960s it was filthy. A redevelopment programme from that decade rebuilt the walls and created the riverside walkway you can see below, and in 2004 the stretch between here and Tazaemonbashi bridge was opened to pedestrians. Photographs from the 1970s show a canal people avoided; you are looking at a cleanup that worked.

One local custom you should not imitate: when a local baseball team wins something enormous, people jump off this bridge into the water. The signs asking you not to are there because it has happened, and because the canal is shallower than it looks. The bridge is free, open at all hours, and best after dark, when the signboards opposite light the water and every photograph anyone takes in Osaka seems to be taken from exactly where you are standing.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a public bridge and a public walkway; no ticket, no gate, open at all hours.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best after sunset once the signboards are lit and again early in the morning if you want the bridge to yourself.
stops.accessibility: The bridge is level and step-free, though it is extremely crowded in the evening. The riverside walkways below are reached by stairs or ramps depending on the section, and the walkway surfaces are paved and flat.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the riverside promenade under the bridge instead of fighting the deck above — it runs east toward Tazaemonbashi and gives you the signboards at water level, which is where the reflections are. Then come back up for the view from the bridge itself.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn on the bridge until you are facing west, downstream, and look at the lit building on the south bank a few dozen metres away, where a runner in blue is frozen mid-stride. Walk down off the bridge and along the canal-side pavement toward it — about thirty metres. You are heading for the base of the sign.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Glico Running Man Sign
stops.narration:
This is probably the most photographed advertisement in Japan, and it started as a boast about calories. In 1935 the confectionery company Ezaki Glico put up a giant illuminated sign here to sell caramel, and the selling line was that one piece gave you enough energy to run three hundred metres — three hundred metres, or three hundred calories, the number doing the work. Hence the runner: a man with both arms raised, crossing a finish line on a blue track. Glico's own company history records that the first version was 33 metres tall. Everything you see now is the sixth generation, installed in October 2014: the first of them to use LEDs rather than neon, about 20 metres high and roughly 10 metres wide, running on something like 140,000 LED chips and normally lit from around six in the evening until midnight. If that sounds oddly modest against the old sign, it is because the site changed rather than the ambition.

The sign is not a monument to the company so much as a barometer of the city. It has been temporarily redesigned to mark World Cup tournaments and to celebrate the Hanshin Tigers, Osaka's baseball team, whose fortunes the whole city takes personally — there is a well-known curse attached to them and a statue of a fried-chicken mascot at the bottom of a river, and if you ask a local about either you will lose twenty minutes and enjoy it. Glico's global fame rests on Pocky; Osaka's affection rests on this.

Watch how people behave in front of it. Almost everyone strikes the same pose — one leg back, both arms up — which makes the sign one of the few pieces of corporate advertising in the world that the public has collectively adopted as a gesture.

The neighbouring billboards are the supporting cast and worth two minutes each: a mechanical crab six and a half metres across, mounted over the Kani Dōraku crab restaurant and still moving its legs and eyestalks, and the ferris wheel set into the face of a discount store across the water — a wheel that ran for years, then sat broken for a decade from 2008 before reopening in 2018 after a ¥250 million repair. This is a district that thinks a building without a moving animal on it is unfinished.

Before you move on, sort out the three dishes Osaka is judged on — all of them konamon, the flour-based cooking of a merchant town. Takoyaki are batter spheres with a piece of octopus inside, poured into a moulded iron pan and turned with a pick; they were invented here in 1935 by a street vendor named Tomekichi Endo, whose original shop still serves them with no sauce at all. Okonomiyaki is the savoury cabbage pancake cooked on the griddle in front of you: in Osaka the ingredients are mixed into the batter, in Hiroshima they are layered instead, and in Tokyo the same tradition turns into monjayaki, a runnier batter you scrape off with tiny spatulas. Kushikatsu is anything breaded, skewered and deep-fried, and the rule is one dip only in the shared sauce tray — the sign on the wall is not decorative.

Nothing here is ticketed; it is a billboard on a public street, free to look at at any hour, with the lights typically going off around midnight. The best photographs are from the canal walkway below and a little to the side, in the hour after sunset when the sky still holds some colour and before the crowds thicken. In February you may want to keep moving rather than stand: the canal wind is cold and there is nowhere to sit. Verify the lighting hours on the day — they change with events.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a public billboard on an open street — nothing to buy and no ticket.
stops.openingHours: Visible at all hours; the LEDs are typically illuminated from around 18:00 until about midnight, with the hours changed for events and power-saving. Check on the night.
stops.accessibility: The pavement and canal walkway in front of the sign are level and step-free, but the riverside path is reached by steps in places and the area is dense with people in the evening. Viewing from the bridge deck is easier than the walkway.
stops.insiderTip: Skip the contest for the middle of the bridge. Shoot instead from the canal walkway below and to the west, where the sign reflects in the water and the crowd is only one deep — then look along the bank at the mechanical crab and the ferris wheel, which most people photograph only in the background.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn inland, away from the canal, and walk south-east into the warren of lanes behind Dōtonbori Street. Hozenji Yokochō is about 250 metres away, three or four minutes — head for the narrow stone-paved alley just south-east of the Dōtonbori shopping street, marked by a wooden gate and a small sign. It is easy to walk straight past; the entrance is barely wider than a doorway.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Tokumeigakarinoaoshima, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hōzenji Yokochō & Mizukake Fudō
stops.narration:
Step off the main street and the noise drops by half. This is Hōzenji Yokochō, a lane of about eighty metres, paved in stone and hung with lanterns, lined with small restaurants and bars — and it is one of the very few pieces of prewar Minami that survived. Minami means simply south, and it is what Osakans call the southern downtown, as opposed to Kita, the north; the two names cover the city's two entertainment hearts. That the lane survived is not because anyone protected it. It survived because the air raids of March 1945 burned this district flat and, for a few years afterwards, nobody had the money to rebuild it into anything bigger. Preservation here was a side effect of poverty, and the lane's charm is exactly that: low wooden frontages, a stone floor, and nowhere to put a glass tower.

The temple at the end, Hōzenji, was founded in 1637, when this area was already the city's theatre and pleasure quarter — the kabuki and puppet stages were a few minutes' walk away, and this lane was full of teahouses and vaudeville theatres and, by the early twentieth century, one of Osaka's first cinemas. The temple was dedicated to Fudō Myō-ō, whose name repays unpacking. In Buddhist thought Fudō Myō-ō — Acala in Sanskrit, the Immovable One — is one of the Five Wisdom Kings, a wrathful guardian whose anger is directed entirely at obstacles to enlightenment; he is the deity you call on for discipline. His conventional image is severe, usually with a sword and a rope and a scowl.

This one is different, and the reason is visitors. The statue of Fudō Myō-ō here, flanked by two smaller attendants, is covered head to toe in dense green moss, to the point that the stone beneath is barely visible. The tradition is called mizukake Fudō — water-splashing Fudō — and it started after the war: a woman came to pray, scooped up water that had been offered at the altar and poured it over the statue, and the wish, or so the story goes, came true. Now everyone does it. Decades of daily watering have produced the moss, which turns a fierce guardian into something that looks, frankly, like a hedge. There are wooden ladles and a water basin; the practice is to pour a little, make your request, and put the ladle back. It costs nothing and there is no correct wording.

The War left the temple with almost nothing — the main hall, the gates and the records all burned — and the statue survived standing alone in the ashes. The neighbourhood noticed. When a place has lost everything and one stone is still upright, that stone takes on a job.

The temple grounds are free and open at all hours, which is itself notable; the alley's restaurants and bars are not, and most open in the evening and charge what a Dōtonbori-adjacent address charges. If you want to eat here rather than look, arrive after six and expect to pay for the atmosphere — verify menus at the door, as prices are not posted anywhere and the small places fill fast. Photographs are welcome in the lane and of the statue, but quiet is the convention in the temple yard, and people do come here specifically to pray.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The temple and the lane are free, with no ticket and no gate. The restaurants and bars along the alley are separate businesses at their own prices — verify at the door, and note that some add a seating charge.
stops.openingHours: The lane and temple courtyard are open access at all hours. The alley's restaurants and bars mostly open in the evening and run late; some close one day a week.
stops.accessibility: The lane is level and paved but narrow, and at night it is dim, crowded and slick when wet — take it slowly. The temple yard itself is flat and step-free; the entrance is a gap in the frontage that is easy to miss.
stops.insiderTip: Come back after dark on a wet evening if you can arrange the weather: the lanterns reflect in the wet flagstones and the alley looks exactly like the photographs, which are usually taken in the rain. Pour water on Fudō before you leave — that is the tradition, not a superstition to be embarrassed about.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the end of the walk, and you are well placed to eat. Stay in the alley if you want a small counter and a bill to match, or step back out to Dōtonbori Street for takoyaki, okonomiyaki or kushikatsu — the three dishes Osaka is judged on. If you are heading home, Osaka Metro Namba station is about five minutes west and Nippombashi, where you started, is about eight minutes north: Namba gives you the Midosuji, Yotsubashi and Sennichimae lines, Nippombashi the Sennichimae and Sakaisuji. Mind the last trains, which run shortly after midnight; the district stays lit long after the platform gates close.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Choi2451, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
